SUMMARY

Bank of America Corporation(BAC-5.20%)reported financial results for the third quarter characterized by growth in its "Main Street" banking segments, which countered headwinds in its capital markets and trading operations. Management reported that strong momentum in consumer banking and wealth management, specifically through checking account expansion and increased advisory flows, drove net interest income and asset management fee growth. The quarter's results were significantly impacted by a non-tax-deductible regulatory settlement charge related to historical compliance issues, though officials indicated that remediation costs are largely incorporated into the current expense run rate. Despite market volatility and its effect on fixed-income trading, the company maintained a strong balance sheet, improved its net interest yield, and continued to return substantial capital to shareholders through dividends and buybacks.

Operator:Hello, and welcome everyone joining today's Bank of America earnings announcement. At this time, all participants are in a listen-only mode. Later, you will have the opportunity to ask questions during the question-and-answer session. You may register to ask a question at any time by pressing star one on your telephone keypad. Please note this call is being recorded. We are standing by if you should need any assistance. It is now my pleasure to turn the meeting over to Lee McEntire of Bank of America.

Lee McEntire:Thank you, [Leo]. Good morning, everyone, and thanks for joining us to talk through our third quarter results. I am joined by Brian Moynihan, our Chair and CEO, and Alastair Borthwick, our CFO. As always, the earnings release and presentation are posted on the investor relations section of bankofamerica.com, and we will reference those materials during the call. Before we begin, a quick reminder, during the call, we may make forward-looking statements and refer to non-GAAP financial measures. These reflect management's current views and are subject to risks and uncertainties. Those are outlined along with the relevant GAAP reconciliations in our earnings materials and SEC filings on our website. With that, I will turn it over to you, Brian.

Brian Moynihan:Morning, and thank you for joining us today. Our third quarter results show the importance of a diversified company. The businesses closest to customers, wealth clients, and commercial clients, the Main Street businesses, show continued strength, higher loans and deposits, strong wealth management flows, higher NII, and better credit drove solid earnings. While the sales and trading revenue, investment banking revenue were lower. We reported net income of $6.9 billion after tax and earnings per share of $0.91. On slide two, we have adjusted those results to take into account the non-tax deductible regulatory settlement charge of $1.2 billion, which is a $0.17 per share impact. Three points to understand about the settlement.

We understand the seriousness of compliance, and we are responsible for getting it right. Second, we have invested billions of dollars in technology and dedicated thousands of employees to combat financial crime. The team is far along with and committed to completing the work required to be addressed by the regulators. Third, we have committed the resources, and the ongoing cost remediation is embedded in our company's expense base. Excluding the regulatory settlement charge, our net income was $8.1 billion, or approximately $1.08 per share, up from last year. Our leadership across our businesses and products and geographies allows us to meet more of each client's needs, deepen relationships, and drive growth across our company.

The connectivity between business units is strong and continues to be a competitive advantage. When we think about our results, it starts with the health and activity of our clients, which brings us to slide three. We believe at Bank of America, our clearest economic signal comes from the daily activity of the 70 million clients and thousands of businesses that bank with us. The message has been consistent. Consumers continue to spend, with year-to-date money movement up 5% from 2025, and you can see that on slide three, and that is similar to what it was for the third quarter and similar to what has shown up so far in early October.

Our business clients invested and hired selectively, supported solid growth in jobs and wages across various income levels in our customer base. Wealth clients remain engaged and continue to seek advice, while commercial clients use more of our lending, treasury, and payments capabilities. Payment volumes, digital activity, loan demand, and wealth flows all remained healthy. You can see the digital activity in the slides in the appendix, as we always put in our results. The economic uncertainty that prevails and the geopolitical instability are always present. What our clients are actually doing is continuing to point to a resilient and growing economy in the U.S.

That activity has produced organic growth across our company, coupled with great credit quality, and we show that in slide four. Slide four shows an addition of organic growth for the quarter. In quarter three, once again, we grew through both client acquisition and doing more with our current client customers. We added another 200,000 in the quarter of net new core consumer checking accounts. We now have 39 million checking account customers. It has been nearly eight straight years of quarterly progress and growth. That is quite a flywheel. We opened more than 1 million new card accounts. Importantly, we grew our card balances nearly 5%, consistent with our medium-term goals disclosed at Investor Day.

The focus on investment in that card product is producing results. Our wealth clients generated approximately $41 billion of flows during the quarter. We continue to add affluent and high-net-worth relationships across global wealth and consumer investments. Across those businesses, clients entrust us with more than $5.7 trillion of their families' balances. Commercial loans grew across every single segment, from small business to business banking to global commercial banking to global corporate investment banking. That is from small businesses to largest companies in the world. Our treasury services, i.e. cash management relationships, also expanded.

This bodes well for our loan growth that we will talk about later, but also shows you the strength in the economy as these commercial customers continue to be active. Growth that you see on this page reflects the investments in our people, our technology, our capabilities in digital, and our physical network. These deep relationships support earnings, balance sheet growth, and long-term shareholder value. With that overview, let me turn it over to Alastair for more detail on the quarter.

Alastair Borthwick:Thanks, Brian. I'll start with a few other income statement highlights on slide five As Brian said, momentum continued in our core banking businesses. Consumer banking, wealth management, and global banking's commercial businesses drove most of the revenue and earnings growth, while markets and investment banking revenue declined from prior periods. Equities delivered a record third quarter, and reduced client activity and changing market conditions, including a major shift in interest rates, significantly affected our leading FICC micro businesses, including credit mortgages and municipals. Those declines more than offset growth elsewhere in trading.

Revenue is approximately $30 billion, up around 3% year-over-year, and an 8% increase in NII and 17% growth in asset management fees more than offset lower investment banking and sales and trading revenue. NII reached $16.6 billion on an FTE basis, up 8% year-over-year, and was up $450 million from the second quarter. Net interest yield of 2.16% improved 15 basis points year-over-year and 8 basis points from the prior quarter, moving us closer to the 2.3% medium-term target we outlined at Investor Day. Credit quality improved, capital and liquidity remained strong, and earnings remained solid.

Let's turn to the balance sheet on slide six, where you can see we remained strong and became more efficient as evidenced by the improvement in our net interest yield. Total assets were $3.4 trillion. That was down 2% from Q2. Ending deposits increased $14 billion from Q2 and remained above $2 trillion. Quarter-end loans rose $34 billion to $1.25 trillion, and we funded that growth by reducing securities balances, while lower markets assets and higher deposits allowed us to reduce short-term wholesale funding, thereby continuing to improve the net interest yield. Loans have now grown for 10 consecutive quarters, reflecting continued activity across both commercial and consumer clients.

Global liquidity sources remained strong at $914 billion, and capital stayed well above regulatory minimums. CET1 was 10.9%, down roughly 35 basis points from Q2, primarily reflecting higher funded and unfunded loans and a $3 billion reduction in CET1 capital. Capital distributions exceeded net income due to the regulatory settlement charge, and we also had a $1.8 billion portion of AOCI of AFS securities that impacted CET1 from higher rates. Our hedging continued to limit the AOCI effect of higher long-term rates on much of the AFS securities portfolio, and a little less than half of the total Q3 AOCI decline related to cash flow hedges and did not affect CET1.

Despite the AOCI impact, tangible common equity ratio, or TCE ratio, was stable with the second quarter. We returned $8.3 billion to shareholders this quarter through dividends and share repurchases, and this combination of balance sheet strength and capital generation continues to support clients and shareholders. Let's turn to deposits on slide seven, where you can see they're at $2 trillion now, up $31 billion from the third quarter of 2025, despite our intentional runoff of $11 billion of higher-cost deposits recorded in all other. Global banking deposits grew 6%, and consumer deposits increased modestly with low interest and non-interest-bearing balances up nearly 3%. GWIM deposits remained stable and well-priced.

Our deposit mix remained attractive, with non-interest-bearing deposits accounting for more than 75% of year-over-year deposit growth. We also remain disciplined on pricing with the total deposit rate rising just 3 basis points to 1.49%. Our focus on operating deposits and our low loan-to-deposit ratio allow us to compete on capabilities rather than price. Clients value the safety and convenience we provide, and a significant share of balances remains in relationship-based operating accounts and other low-cost funding. Our deposit franchise remains an important competitive advantage for us and continues to fund healthy client activity. Let's turn to the loan trends Brian mentioned on slide eight. Here we show average loans up approximately 6% year-over-year, led by broad-based gains in commercial.

Wealth-related lending also remained strong, and card balance growth continued to improve. Commercial loans increased 8% year-over-year, with growth across every line of business, with small business up 2%, business banking up 9%, global commercial up 6%, global corporate up 10%, and GWIM custom lending was up 22%. Within that performance, global banking international commercial loans grew 15%. Further, we saw broad-based middle-market growth across the commercial banking segments in key sectors including real estate, sports, technology, healthcare, and biopharmaceuticals. In consumer, card balances grew nearly 5%, while higher consumer real estate balances and small business growth were more than offset by lower auto balances. Securities-based lending and wealth management grew 21%.

Fortunately, the growth remains consistent with our underwriting standards and credit discipline. It also supported another strong quarter for net interest income, which we show on slide nine. As I noted earlier, both net interest income of $16.6 billion and the net interest yield were up strongly from both Q2 and a year ago. Fixed-rate asset repricing and global markets activity both remain contributors, and commercial loans, card balances, and deposits have increasingly been the ones driving the growth. Looking forward, we expect NII to improve sequentially in Q4 and again through 2027 based on anticipated modest loan and deposit growth and continued fixed-rate asset repricing.

This outlook also assumes three 25-basis points rate increases through June of 2027, so in December 2026 and March and June of next year. At Investor Day last year, we shared an expectation we would deliver 5%-7% NII growth in the medium term. During the course of 2026, we've raised that guidance first to 7% and then more recently to 8%. We still expect to hit that full-year revised NII growth guidance of approximately 8%. For 2027, we currently expect full-year growth of NII to be 8% or more, higher than 2026, and again, higher than our original 5%-7% range. The banking book remains asset sensitive.

On a dynamic deposit basis, a 100-basis points parallel shift above the forward curve would be expected to increase NII by $1.4 billion over the following 12 months, and that's a touch higher than the second quarter. When we turn to slide 10, we see expense. We reported expense of $19.7 billion, and that included the $1.2 billion regulatory settlement charge. Excluding that charge, adjusted expense was a little more than $18.5 billion, down nearly $100 million from Q2 and up slightly less than 7% from a year ago. The year-over-year increase reflected higher revenue-related costs in asset management and equities, including incentive compensation in wealth management and brokerage clearing and exchange costs in equities, respectively.

We also invested in technology modernization, AI, client acquisition, marketing, and franchise growth. At the same time, productivity continues to improve, as evidenced by our headcount. Even as we add headcount in our sales forces, our headcount was down nearly 3,500 from a year ago as we automate processes and simplify work across the company. This means we don't need to hire quite as many people to refill roles. We remain focused on investing where we see the best long-term returns while we continue to improve the productivity of the organization. We expect to return to operating leverage in Q4. From expense, let's move to credit quality on slides 11 and 12.

Here you can see the credit quality remains stable and in fact improved modestly once again this quarter. Provision expense was approximately $1.3 billion, lower than Q2, and the net charge-off ratio improved to 44 basis points. Consumer credit improved in line with expectations. The 3.22% card loss rate improved from Q2 and along with delinquencies declined for the sixth consecutive quarter on a year-over-year basis. Commercial criticized assets declined to their lowest level on a rate basis since 4Q 2019, and non-performing loans also fell from Q2. Together, these trends continue to point to a healthy consumer and commercial client base and credit quality.

With that credit backdrop, let's now turn to each business, beginning with consumer banking on slide 13. Consumer delivered another solid quarter, combining the organic client growth and disciplined execution with continued investment in the franchise. Revenue rose about 4% to $11.6 billion, and net income increased about 2% to $3.5 billion. Year-to-date results remain robust, with revenue up 5% and net income up 10%. Year-over-year expense comparisons are tougher because we increased marketing beginning in the fourth quarter of 2025, ahead of new sponsorships and the relaunch of BofA Rewards, with spending steady for the past four quarters. We opened 14 financial centers this quarter and plan to open about another 20 or more by year-end.

Since its May relaunch, BofA Rewards has enrolled nearly 6 million clients, deepening engagement across banking, cards, and investments. As a result of these investments, we've seen continued account openings and non-interest-bearing deposit growth, higher new card originations and card balance growth, and higher digital engagement and client satisfaction. The business produced a 50% efficiency ratio and a 31% return on allocated capital. In consumer, it's our deposit franchise that remains a key strength, with average deposits of about $949 billion, marking a sixth consecutive quarter of year-over-year growth. Non-interest-bearing deposits grew more than 4%, while 59% of balances remained in checking accounts, and 92% of those relationships were primary accounts.

Consumer investment assets reached $664 billion, up 14%, supported by market gains and about $18 billion of net flows over the past year. Digital adoption reached new highs with over 50 million active users. 80% of consumer households are digitally active, and digital channels generated 71% of sales. Erica, Zelle, and AI-enabled tools are helping clients and helping employees to complete more activity faster and more consistently. That mix of relationship growth, digital engagement, and disciplined execution continues to strengthen consumer banking. Turning to wealth management now on slide 14. This business continued to improve profitability through strong client flows, positive operating leverage, and higher margins.

Revenue rose about 13% to $7.1 billion, and net income increased 22% to more than $1.5 billion. Pre-tax margin approached 29%, return on allocated capital reached about 28%, and operating leverage was strongly positive as client activity and market levels lifted asset management fees and NII. Client balances climbed above $5 trillion for the first time, up 9%, while AUM rose 12% to about $2.4 trillion. Quarterly net client flows were about $38 billion, including approximately $20 billion of AUM flows, bringing four-quarter AUM flows to about $74 billion. Growth was broad-based.

Merrill added about 4,200 net new households with at least $500,000 in assets, up 17%, and the private bank added 417 net new relationships with at least $3 million under management. These results reflect strong demand for advice and our ability to attract clients and experienced advisors to the platform. Banking relationships also deepened, as now 67% of Merrill clients have banking relationships with us. Ending loans rose about 12% to more than $280 billion, led by securities-based lending, custom lending, and mortgages. Private bank lending has now grown for 12 consecutive quarters as clients use more of our investment and banking capabilities.

Advisor productivity, disciplined pricing, digital engagement, and AI tools continue to expand our capacity to deliver personalized advice at scale. That sustained organic growth leads us to global banking on slide 15. Global banking segment benefited from strong loan and deposit growth and treasury activity, which helped offset softer investment banking results. Year to date, the commercial bank added more than 300 new companies and logos, and in September, we launched a GenAI tool designed to make prospecting and onboarding even more efficient. Revenue of $6.2 billion was relatively flat year-over-year, and net income was just under $2 billion, down modestly year-over-year. However, strong pipelines and the broader year-to-date performance put this quarter's investment banking results in context.

Year-to-date, global banking revenue is up 5%, net income is up 7%, and the total company investment banking fees are up 16%. Return on allocated capital was 15%, and balance sheet growth reflected the continued client momentum. Average deposits rose 6% year-over-year to $669 billion. Average loans increased 8% to $419 billion, and ending loans came in at $428 billion. Growth was broad-based across commercial and corporate clients. Treasury services revenue increased 10% as we helped clients manage liquidity, payments, and working capital while creating more opportunities across lending, investment banking, and global markets. Total company investment banking fees, excluding self-led transactions, were about $1.8 billion.

Fees declined from a strong year-ago period, driven by lower advisory and debt underwriting fees. Looking forward, our pipelines remained healthy. We continue to invest in bankers, technology, and AI tools in an effort to improve research, preparation, and opportunity identification. That broad client connectivity also supports global markets, which we cover on slide 16. Here you can see solid results despite a tough comparison in our FICC credit businesses with slower trading activity this year. Excluding DVA, revenue was $5.8 billion, and net income was $1.2 billion, both down from Q3 2025. Even so, the year-to-date performance remains a record for the firm, with revenue up 11% and net income up 14%.

Sales and trading revenue, excluding DVA, was $5.1 billion, down 5% year-over-year. It was a record third quarter for equities, and it was a record third quarter for international revenue. Equities revenue rose 10% to $2.5 billion, led by prime financing and strong client activity. The results reflect our investments in talent, technology, and financing capabilities over time. FICC revenue was $2.5 billion, down 17%. FX and commodities benefited from increased client activity, lifting our macro businesses 4%. That strength was more than offset by lower activity in mortgages, municipals, and credit following a strong year-ago period.

The expense increase may seem counterintuitive given the revenue decline, but it reflects higher transaction costs tied to the equities growth, particularly in prime financing and in Asia, reflecting our continued long-term investment and expansion. Average loans rose 5%, demonstrating stronger financing relationships and connectivity across markets, global banking, and wealth management. With the business segments results covered, let's finish with all other and some closing thoughts on slide 17. All other reported a loss of $1.4 billion, and that obviously includes the $1.2 billion regulatory settlement charge, which is not tax-deductible. Excluding the regulatory settlement charge, all other shows a loss of $153 million compared with a loss of $103 million a year ago.

The overall effective tax rate was 23%, and excluding the regulatory settlement charge, the adjusted effective tax rate was closer to 20%. Let me close then with some key takeaways from the quarter. Customers continued to spend, supporting a resilient U.S. economy, while wealth clients brought in assets to us and relied on us for advice. Business clients kept spending, borrowing, investing, and growing, and institutional clients remain active globally, even though at a slower pace. Those trends were evident across the company and drove another solid quarter. Our pipelines and our client conversations reflect the same confidence we have in the economy, even as clients keep a close eye on geopolitical uncertainty.

Our balance sheet and capital remain strong, and we continue to invest in technology and develop AI capabilities to support long-term growth. This quarter demonstrates the strength of our franchise and the value of our diversified business model. With that, I'll say thank you, and we'll stop now to take your questions.

Operator:Thank you. If you'd like to ask a question, press star one on your keypad. To leave the queue at any time, please press star two. Once again, that is star one to ask a question, and we'll pause for just a moment to allow everyone a chance to join the queue. Thank you. Our first question comes from Chris McGratty with KBW. Please go ahead. Your line is open.

Chris McGratty:Oh, great. Good morning. Brian or Alastair, on the capital outlook, you talked about modest balance sheet growth. I'm wondering if you could dig into your assumptions between growth of the balance sheet and returning of capital balancing the CET1 and the TCE ratio. Thanks.

Alastair Borthwick:Sure. Well, first, I'd say if you look at the course of the year, we've obviously supported all the client growth that we've seen with the capital that we generate. If we look at where we stand today, we've obviously got a considerable amount of flexibility on capital, just recognizing that we're at 10.9% CET1 and a reg minimum at 10%. We also generate substantial capital. If you look at this quarter, for example, Chris, we supported $34 billion in loan growth. We obviously had a regulatory penalty. We saw rates go up 85 basis points. We paid an increased dividend, and we bought back $6 billion in shares.

So we've got a lot of flexibility with the earnings that we generate to balance exactly what we've been doing through the course of this year and over the course of time. Always our priority is going to be support the clients and the growth. We know we have to support the regulatory minimum and the dividend, and then whatever is left, we're going to return to shareholders. So no change.

Chris McGratty:Okay, great. On the operating leverage comment, Q4, heard you there, but could we revisit 2027? You gave us a pretty good NII update. I think the guided Investor Day was 200-300 basis points. Any changes of how you're feeling about that going into next year?

Alastair Borthwick:No. No change there. We've obviously had a very good first half. Q3 was slower, and we're back on creating operating leverage in Q4. I think as we get into Q4, Chris, I will likely provide guidance for next year, but it's not going to change from the 200-300 basis points. Based on what we see, it could be higher. But we'll see as we get closer.

Chris McGratty:Thank you.

Operator:Thank you. We'll move on now to David Chiaverini with Jefferies. Your line is open.

David Chiaverini:Hi. Thanks for taking the questions. Wanted to touch on the NII guide of 8%+ looking out to next year. I was curious on the drivers behind the improvement. Is it all rate driven or anything else driving that improvement?

Alastair Borthwick:No, it's not all rates. Rates are obviously a small component of that. But same drivers as this year, David. We've seen a little more normal deposit growth this year, and particularly where we've seen it is in non-interest bearing. So if you look at the non-interest bearing in consumer or you look at the non-interest bearing in global banking, that's returned to something a little more normal. We'd always thought deposit growth should be in kind of the 4%-5% in a normal type economy. And that's kind of where the non-interest bearing is now over the course of the last year-over-year. So that's number one. Number two, the pricing rotation is slowing.

So we've seen, for example, consumers flattened out. It's now grown six quarters in a row. Wealth management, same thing. The loan growth has kind of averaged $20 billion a quarter over the course of time. We don't see that slowing at this point in time. Then we've talked about we benefit from fixed rate asset repricing, most notably in the auto loan and the residential mortgage portfolios, but also in our mortgage-backed securities and our cash flow swaps. If anything, in the last quarter just increased both floating rate yields and fixed rate yields. So do rates help us as we look into 2027? Yes. But it's the core underlying growth in deposits and loans that help us.

Then I think that we have to recognize in 2027, if rates go up, we would expect global markets, it's liability sensitive. It's entirely possible that global markets will go down. But remember, we continue to add loans in global markets, and we continue to invest in global markets. So that will offset that just a little bit. The gains in banking are going to more than offset that. That's the core part. The core banking book is going to be stronger in 2027 than 2026.

Brian Moynihan:Yeah. To be precise, the 8% includes effectively a drag on markets because it hasn't been growing for the last couple of quarters. It's been relatively flat. So it's an all-in number overcoming that, just to be clear.

David Chiaverini:Great. Thanks for that. On the consent order, are there any constraints or does this impede business operations in any way as we look forward?

Alastair Borthwick:Just repeat me your question one more time. I am sorry. I was writing a note to myself. Go ahead.

David Chiaverini:Sure. Just on the consent order.

Alastair Borthwick:Yes.

David Chiaverini:Are there any constraints on the business? Does it impede your normal business operations at all?

Alastair Borthwick:No, there is no asset cap here, so no, there is nothing there. In terms of it will not crowd out anything either because we have invested the technology and we have invested the people that we feel like we need to get the work done. So that is in the run rate. We have made the decisions we need to. We have added the resources we feel like we need. So it should not impact our clients in any way.

David Chiaverini:Great. Thanks very much.

Operator:Thank you. We'll move next to Manan Gosalia with Morgan Stanley. Your line is now open.

Manan Gosalia:Hi. Good morning. On the consumer side, you noted that consumers continue to spend, and consumers are healthy. Maybe you can give us some more color on what you're seeing there with short-end rates moving higher for longer gas prices. Are you seeing any signs of pressure? Are there any changes that you're making at the margin in terms of where you're leaning in or leaning out?

Brian Moynihan:Let's separate two things. One, on the credit quality, our underwriting standards are consistent to 5% growth. Credit cards is with the same underwriting standards, and you can see the stats, very strong. The charge-offs there, 3% and change. We feel very good about that. Any other consumer loan quality metrics continue to be strong and improve. In terms of seeing any stress in the consumer, absolutely not in terms of credit quality. Then if you go to the balance in our accounts as they're growing, and we look at the paychecks, the direct deposits coming from employers to our consumers, we see those growing across the three segments of income.

We have low, medium, and high, and we see the low having picked up. That all bodes well. When you go to actually what their activity is, as we said on the slide, is 5% more spending this year than last year. Yes, gas spending is up 20-odd percent. When you look at the credit and debit card spending only, that does crowd out. As you look at some of the online data, you can see the gas spending and the inside store spending is still growing in the convenience stores, but not quite at the rate that it was. So it crowds out a little bit. But frankly, it's really different stories for different types of people.

In the overall positioning, the rest of the spending is very strong at the 5% and on entertainment and other categories that you see there.

Manan Gosalia:Got it. Then if you could give us some more color on the positive operating leverage for next year. What are the key drivers? Clearly you're dropping more of the NII growth to the bottom line, so that's certainly a positive. But if you could talk about some of the levers that you have on the expense side and if you could clarify that the 200-300 basis points is on the adjusted expense number for 2026 excluding the settlement charge.

Alastair Borthwick:Well, I think that's the best way to look at it because we wouldn't view that as being a repeated. We view that as a one time. It's not a core operating expense, so I think you've got to adjust for that. But yes, we still feel like 200-300 basis points is generally speaking the right kind of a zone. We put that out for Investor Day through the medium term. We'll get into what we want to guide for 2027 when we get into the fourth quarter. But you've identified the first thing, which is NII growth. A lot of it drops straight to the bottom line, and that's really important. That's a very powerful driver for our company.

Then obviously we've got some terrific opportunities to continue to grow the fee businesses as we have consistently invested there. So we've got a good opportunity across the board, we feel like, whether it's wealth, global banking, and global markets to keep driving the fee side. So that we feel good about. Then on the expense, we've got a pretty good track record of headcount management all the way through this year. So if you look at what we've done in terms of what's the main driver of expense for any business, 60%-70% of it is headcount. We've done a nice job of managing headcount with discipline all year.

We're going to maintain that management discipline into next year that allows us to create the operating leverage that we're talking about. Final thing I'll just say is we obviously benefit a great deal from the fact that we've got a consumer business, a wealth business, small business, medium-sized business, large businesses, and investors. And the interconnectedness of those, the flows of business that go between them, is another thing we've highlighted at Investor Day presentation and afterwards, and another area of additional growth for us that we continue to explore.

Manan Gosalia:Great. Thank you.

Operator:Thank you. We'll move on now to Ben Gerlinger with Citi. Your line is now open. Please go ahead.

Ben Gerlinger:Hi. Good morning. I just wanted to double-check. So you have the full year NII, and then next year's is also strong. Then you also say that non-interest-bearing deposit growth has been healthy. So are you kind of assuming that non-interest-bearing deposit growth continues to be healthy despite the three additional hikes your forward expectations include? If so, can you also unpack some of the deposit betas you might be assuming in next year's NII?

Alastair Borthwick:Yep. First, with respect to non-interest-bearing. Yep, we're assuming low single digits for deposit growth broadly, and we're anticipating that we can continue to grow non-interest-bearing deposits as we have done over the course of the past year. Remember, whether rates go up by 25 basis points or not, at some point, non-interest-bearing deposits are impacted more by inflation and GDP. So we ought to see continued growth in non-interest-bearing deposits through the course of time. A lot of the rotation of rates took place when rates went from 25 basis points to 4.5%. We've been in that environment now for three or four years.

There's been a lot of time for consumers and wealthy clients to sort of settle into that environment. Yes, we anticipate continued growth in our deposits. In terms of deposit betas, obviously we came from 4.5% down to 3.75%, 3.50%. Now we're retracing steps. I would anticipate it'll look the same going back up as it did coming down. The areas to watch continue to be obviously in consumer. It's about CD pricing. In wealth, we tend to pass along pricing with interest rate hikes and cuts. The same thing is true in global banking. When the Fed raises rates, we're typically passing that through to our clients.

So there'll be no change in our perspective on the way back up as there was originally, nor in the way that we think about it on the way down. So no change there.

Ben Gerlinger:Got it. Thank you.

Operator:Thank you. We'll move next to John McDonald with Truist Securities. Your line is now open.

John McDonald:Thanks. Good morning. Brian, I was hoping you could give a little perspective in terms of the OCC and FinCEN orders, like how it gets to this point.
